item.title: AWS Adds Enhanced Observability to SageMaker HyperPod for GPU Training
item.description:
AWS Adds Enhanced Observability to SageMaker HyperPod for GPU Training

Amazon has announced enhanced observability capabilities for Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, a new feature designed to help users diagnose GPU training issues more quickly. This update introduces diagnostic and profiling tools for training workloads running on both Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) and Slurm orchestrators.

🧩 How it works

The new observability layer combines automated outlier detection with static diagnostic rules to surface common failure patterns before they impact training performance.

  • Diagnostic Summary: Utilizes Amazon CloudWatch’s DetectGroupOutliers API to compare each GPU in a training job. It flags GPUs that deviate from their peers based on utilization, memory, temperature, power, and SM clock.
  • Static Diagnostic Rules: Evaluate known failure patterns and organize detected issues by type:
    • Hardware: GPU ECC memory errors, XID faults, and accelerator failures.
    • Network: EFA throughput degradation, packet drops, and retransmissions.
    • Throttling: GPU clock throttling due to heat, board, or reliability limits.
    • Overheating: GPU temperatures exceeding configured limits.

⚙️ Key details

Enhanced observability collects telemetry at two distinct levels, with options for metric storage that have been updated to include CloudWatch as a default choice.

Metric Level Inclusion Coverage
Default Metrics Enabled automatically Cluster health, CPU/disk/OS-level usage, GPU utilization and temperature, and per-job resource utilization. Collected every 30 seconds with ~1–2% CPU overhead and 250–300 MB memory usage.
Advanced Metrics Opt-in Full node exporter suite (host-level), all NVIDIA GPU DCGM and AWS Neuron metrics (clock speeds, power, PCIe, errors), and Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) metrics (throughput, drops, retransmissions).

Previously, only Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus was supported for metrics. CloudWatch is now the default, offering lower pricing compared to Prometheus and tighter integration with the SageMaker console through CloudWatch SageMaker Insights. Users can still choose Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus if they standardize on Prometheus and Grafana for observability.

💡 Why it matters

This capability is delivered as an add-on for EKS-orchestrated clusters and as an extension for Slurm-orchestrated clusters. This structure allows users to control who can install or change the observability layer through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). The “Enable HyperPod Observability” setting is checked by default.

#AWS #SageMaker #HyperPod #GPU #Observability #CloudWatch

Source: Introducing enhanced infrastructure observability in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Using Amazon Bedrock CloudWatch metrics and evals for LLM observability
item.description:
Using Amazon Bedrock CloudWatch metrics and evals for LLM observability

Airbnb uses Amazon Bedrock to run its internal coding agent tool, AirChat, and has developed a specific observability workflow that combines AWS CloudWatch metrics with custom evaluations. This approach allows the engineering team to monitor production performance, manage costs, and validate model changes effectively.

🔍 Overview

Amazon Bedrock provides access to foundation models from multiple providers through a common API, with AWS managing the underlying infrastructure. At Airbnb, thousands of engineers use AirChat weekly to run coding agents. These agents send model requests through an internal LLM gateway that runs on Amazon Bedrock, ensuring that Airbnb’s code, prompts, and model responses are processed within AWS. The system integrates with standard AWS access controls and monitoring tools.

⚙️ Key Details

To manage the impact of frequent model updates, Airbnb utilizes a combination of operational metrics and quality evaluations:

  • Evaluations (Evals): Before a new model rollout, the team runs evals on a fixed set of representative tasks to measure the model’s score and cost per task.
  • Production Observability: After a rollout, observability data is used to compare production usage against eval results. If discrepancies exist, the team investigates the cause.
  • Cost Per Task: This is defined as the list-price cost of all tokens an agent uses to finish one task. It serves as a key metric alongside performance scores to determine default model and reasoning effort settings.

CloudWatch Metrics for Bedrock

Most production problems can be diagnosed using specific signals in the AWS/Bedrock namespace in CloudWatch. The following table outlines the key metrics used to monitor latency, throttling, and cost:

Category Metric Description
Latency InvocationLatency Measures time from API call to response.
Latency TimeToFirstToken Time until the first token is generated.
Latency OutputTokenCount Total output tokens generated.
Latency OTPS Output tokens per second (derived metric).
Throttling InvocationThrottles Count of throttled requests.
Throttling EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage Estimated tokens per minute quota consumption, including cache write tokens and output burndown multipliers, across inference APIs.
Cost InputTokenCount Uncached input tokens.
Cost CacheReadInputTokenCount Input tokens read from cache (lower cost than uncached).
Cost CacheWriteInputTokenCount Input tokens written to cache (can have higher cost depending on model).
Cost OutputTokenCount Generated output tokens.

The EstimatedTPMQuotaUsage metric helps teams set proactive alarms, track quota consumption across models, and request quota increases before hitting rate limits. A lower cache hit rate can increase the cost per request due to the pricing differences between uncached input and cache reads.

💡 Why It Matters

In a period of about five weeks, eight new models were released. By mid-October, approximately two-thirds of engineer requests through coding agents were directed to these new models. Each release can simultaneously change output tokens, cost, latency, and capacity. Since published benchmark charts do not always reflect how a model handles specific internal workloads, Airbnb’s approach of running evals on their own tasks and monitoring distinct CloudWatch signals allows them to choose appropriate default models and reasoning effort ceilings for their engineers.

#AmazonBedrock #CloudWatch #LLMObservability #Airbnb #AIEngineering

Source: How Airbnb uses cost per task to operate coding agents on Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Centralized Observability Data Lake Solution Released for Amazon Bedrock Model Invocations
item.description:
Centralized Observability Data Lake Solution Released for Amazon Bedrock Model Invocations

A centralized observability data lake solution has been introduced for Amazon Bedrock model invocations. Built using AWS CloudFormation, AWS Lambda, Amazon Data Firehose, and Amazon Athena, the solution consolidates raw invocation logs across multiple AWS accounts into a single querying location.

🔍 Overview

Amazon Bedrock offers model invocation logging to record requests and responses sent to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon CloudWatch. The centralized data lake pulls raw invocation logs from linked source accounts into a central account, providing an organization-wide clean table that can be queried using ordinary SQL.

⚙️ Captured log details

When an application calls an Amazon Bedrock model, invocation logging records specific request and metadata details:

  • Prompt: The prompt sent by the user or application.
  • Model response: The response returned by the model.
  • Token counts: Input and output token counts to measure invocation weight.
  • Model: The model used, allowing teams to track model utilization.
  • Stop reason: The reason a response concluded (such as max_tokens).
  • Account and timestamp: Attributes used for timing and attribution.
  • IAM identity: The AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role that initiated the prompt.

🧩 Architecture and pipeline

The centralized observability pipeline is deployed repeatably across accounts using two AWS CloudFormation templates as Infrastructure as Code. The pipeline operates as follows:

  1. Logging activation: Invocation logging is enabled per account with a single API call, pointing Amazon Bedrock to a local CloudWatch log group with write permissions.
  2. Subscription filters: Each source account log group uses a subscription filter to forward records to a CloudWatch Logs destination in the central account. Source accounts do not receive permissions on the central pipeline.
  3. Lambda processing: A small AWS Lambda function unwraps batch records into individual log entries and lifts fields to the top level for simple querying.
  4. Buffering and conversion: Amazon Data Firehose buffers the log records, converts them from JSON to Parquet format, files objects under date paths (such as year=2026/month=08/day=27/), and writes them to an Amazon S3 bucket.
  5. Data querying: An AWS Glue table defines the schema so Amazon Athena can expose the data as one clean SQL-queryable table.
Pipeline Component Role in Data Lake Architecture
Amazon CloudWatch Collects raw logs in source accounts and receives forwarded logs in the central account
Subscription Log Filters Routes log records from source accounts to the central CloudWatch destination
AWS Lambda Unwraps record batches and lifts nested fields to top-level attributes
Amazon Data Firehose Buffers data, converts JSON to Parquet, applies date partitioning, and writes to S3
Amazon S3 Stores converted Parquet log data
AWS Glue Defines table schemas for Athena
Amazon Athena Provides single-table SQL query access across the organization

💡 Key capabilities

Using the centralized data lake, organizations can analyze model usage pattern metrics across accounts:

  • Identify which users consume the highest number of tokens.
  • Determine commonly selected models and review prompt text.
  • Connect logging data with the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) to track daily user prompt spend.

Templates, Lambda code, and SQL queries are available in the AWS Sample Bedrock Invocation Data Lake GitHub repository.

#AmazonBedrock #AWS #CloudObservability #DataLake #CloudWatch

Source: Amazon Bedrock tokenomics data lake | Amazon Web Services
